title: Ali Khwajah and the Merchant of Baghdad

full_text:
In the days of Caliph Harun al-Rashid, there lived in Baghdad a devout merchant named Ali Khwajah. Having decided to undertake the holy pilgrimage to Mecca, he sold his household goods and closed his shop.

After paying all debts, he possessed one thousand gold dinars. Not wishing to carry such wealth on perilous desert roads, he placed the gold at the bottom of a large earthen jar, covering it completely with fresh, plump olives.

He carried the jar to an old friend, a reputable olive merchant, saying:
'Brother, I embark upon the pilgrimage tomorrow. Keep this jar of olives safely in your warehouse until my return.'
The friend gave him the keys, pointing to a corner: 'Place it there with your own hands, Ali Khwajah; it shall remain untouched until thou claimest it.'

Ali Khwajah completed the pilgrimage, but finding great trading opportunities, traveled onward to Cairo, Damascus, and Persia, remaining abroad for seven full years.

During the seventh year, the Baghdad merchant's wife expressed a sudden craving for fresh olives. Her husband remembered Ali Khwajah's jar: 'It has stood in my cellar for seven years; the man is surely dead. Let us taste them.'
Opening the jar, he found the top olives moldy and rotten. Pouring them into a basin to check the lower layers, a cascade of golden dinars clattered onto the stone floor!

Temptation overcame the merchant's soul. He scooped the thousand dinars into his private coffer, threw away the spoiled olives, bought fresh green olives from the morning market, filled the jar to the brim, and sealed it with wax.

A month later, Ali Khwajah returned safely to Baghdad. He visited his friend, who returned the jar with warm embraces. But when Ali Khwajah opened it in his lodgings, he found only green olives—the thousand pieces of gold were gone!

He returned to the merchant, pleading quietly: 'Friend, perhaps thou hadst need of the gold? Repay it as a loan when able, and I shall speak no word of it.'
The merchant became indignant: 'Art thou mad? Thou didst place the jar with thine own hands and didst retrieve it sealed! Accuse me not of theft!'

Ali Khwajah took the matter before the Kazi, but having no witnesses and only a sealed jar, the court dismissed the case. Desperate, Ali Khwajah wrote a petition to Caliph Harun al-Rashid.

That evening, the Caliph walked disguised through the streets with Vizier Ja'afar. Passing a courtyard, he saw children playing a courtroom game. A bright boy sat upon a bench as the 'Caliph', another played 'Ali Khwajah', and a third played the 'Dishonest Merchant'.

The child-judge listened carefully, then commanded: 'Bring the jar of olives before me!'
He tasted an olive and said: 'These olives are crisp and fresh! Olive merchants know that olives spoil within three years! How can olives stored for seven years taste fresh from the tree? The jar has been tampered with!'

Harun al-Rashid was struck by the child's brilliant deduction. The next morning, he summoned the boy to the imperial diwan, along with Ali Khwajah, the accused merchant, and two master olive tasters of Baghdad.

The expert tasters sampled the fruit and affirmed: 'Commander of the Faithful, these olives are of this year's harvest; no olive can preserve flavor beyond two seasons.'

Confronted with undeniable proof, the dishonest merchant confessed, wept, and restored the thousand dinars with damages. The Caliph rewarded the clever boy with a purse of gold and an appointment to royal tutorship, establishing the principle that forensic truth cuts through the craftiest perjuries.
moral: Truth has a quiet fragrance that deceit cannot extinguish; youth and clear eyes often perceive justice when adults are blinded by form.
